title: Adaptive Path Planning and Collision Avoidance for Autonomous Vehicles on Unstructured Indian Roads
dataset_link:
Teams may use built-in sensor and scenario datasets available in MathWorks Automated Driving Toolbox, RoadRunner sample scenes, synthetic scenarios created by the team, and publicly available traffic datasets relevant to Indian road conditions.

• Indian Driving Dataset (IDD): https://idd.insaan.iiit.ac.in/
• Mendeley traffic data
description:
Background:
Most autonomous driving systems are developed for roads with clear lane markings, standard signage, predictable traffic flow, and controlled intersections. Indian roads are often very different. Vehicles of many types share the same space, including cars, buses, trucks, auto-rickshaws, twowheelers, bicycles, pedestrians, pushcarts, and animals. Drivers and pedestrians may change direction suddenly, merge without signalling, drive against traffic, or cross at unmarked locations. In many areas, road edges are unclear, potholes are common, and formal lane discipline is limited. These conditions make it difficult for traditional path planning methods that depend on structured road geometry and predictable motion. India has a large and diverse road network that includes village roads, crowded market areas, urban intersections, and highways. To support the safe deployment of autonomous vehicles in such environments, students must build planning systems that can adapt in real time to uncertainty, mixed traffic, and changing road conditions.
Description:
Design and simulate an adaptive path planning system for an autonomous vehicle that operates in unstructured Indian road conditions. The system should perceive the environment using a multi-sensor setup such as camera, LiDAR, and radar, and identify diverse road users and obstacles, including auto-rickshaws, pushcarts, pedestrians, and animals. It should predict the short-term motion of surrounding agents, including non-lane-based and irregular movement patterns, and generate a safe, collision-free path that can be replanned in real time. The solution should also handle practical driving situations such as missing lane markings, informal merging, sudden pedestrian movement, and unexpected obstacles on the road. Teams should validate their solution using at least five realistic Indian road scenarios, such as an unmarked village road, a busy urban intersection without signals, a highway merge involving slow-moving vehicles, a dense market area with mixed traffic, and a sudden cattle-crossing event. Teams are encouraged to use MathWorks tools such as RoadRunner for scenario design, Automated Driving Toolbox for sensor modeling and fusion, Navigation Toolbox and Stateflow for planning and decision logic, Vehicle Dynamics Blockset or a Simulink bicycle model for vehicle behavior, and Deep Learning Toolbox for detection and trajectory prediction.
Expected Solution:
The expected solution should include three main parts.First, teams should build a working simulation pipeline that integrates perception, prediction, path planning, decision logic, and vehicle motion in MATLAB and Simulink. Second, teams should create realistic driving scenarios that represent Indian road conditions, including at least two detailed RoadRunner scenes such as a village road and an urban intersection, and use them to test the vehicle across all five required scenarios. Third, teams should present results that show safe and reliable navigation, including collision-free performance, smooth path generation, and timely replanning during changing road conditions. The final submission should include the simulation model, the designed scenarios, performance results with metrics such as replanning latency, path smoothness, and scenario completion rate, a short technical report that explains the approach and design choices, and a demonstration video that shows the vehicle navigating the test scenarios. The solution should demonstrate closed-loop validation of autonomous driving behavior under realistic mixed-traffic conditions.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on deep learning, autonomous applied to a robotics and drones problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Robotics and Drones. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on sensor, model, standard. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 20/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Adaptive Path Planning and Collision Avoidance for Autonomous Vehicles on Unstructured Indian Roads

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a simulated self-driving system that can navigate India's genuinely chaotic roads, mixed traffic, no lane discipline, sudden direction changes, rather than the clean, predictable roads most autonomous driving research assumes.
overview.why_it_matters: Autonomous vehicle research built for structured Western roads simply won't work in India. Solving for real Indian road chaos is what actually makes autonomous driving viable here.
pain_points: Traditional path planning assumes structured roads with clear lanes and predictable traffic.
Indian roads have mixed vehicle types, unpredictable behavior, and unclear road edges.
Existing autonomous systems aren't designed for this level of uncertainty.
overview.background: Most autonomous driving research targets structured roads with predictable conditions, but Indian roads present mixed traffic, unclear lane discipline, and unpredictable pedestrian/vehicle behavior that standard approaches can't handle.
overview.whats_being_asked: An adaptive path planning and collision avoidance system, simulated, using multi-sensor perception (camera, LiDAR), that operates reliably in unstructured, mixed-traffic Indian road conditions.
expected_solution: Adaptive real-time path planning under uncertainty.
Collision avoidance for mixed, unpredictable traffic.
Simulation-validated performance across varied road scenarios.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Adaptive planning for genuinely unstructured, unpredictable traffic (not just noisy structured traffic) is a real, actively-researched robotics challenge, not solved by standard autonomous-driving approaches.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Multi-sensor fusion, real-time adaptive planning, and collision avoidance together represent one of the more technically demanding PS in the batch, though it's explicitly framed as simulation, which meaningfully de-risks it versus a physical build.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine robotics/autonomous-systems expertise (this PS is from MathWorks, likely expects MATLAB/Simulink-based simulation), a narrower, more technical field than typical PS.

innovation.note: Genuinely addresses an active robotics research gap, unstructured-environment planning, rather than a solved problem.

invention.note: Multi-sensor fusion plus adaptive planning plus collision avoidance is substantial technical depth.

technical_feasibility.note: No physical vehicle/hardware needed, this is a software simulation challenge, which is far more achievable in 36 hours than a physical build.

impact_and_benefits.note: Solving for Indian road conditions specifically addresses a real gap in autonomous vehicle research relevance to India.

architecture.note: Sensor simulation, perception, and planning algorithms need to work together, but within one simulation environment, no physical-system integration risk.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with robotics/simulation skills, especially MATLAB/Simulink experience given the sponsoring organization. Being explicitly a simulation task (not physical hardware) significantly de-risks feasibility relative to how technically deep the problem is.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Framed explicitly as simulation, not a physical build, this removes the hardware-sourcing risk that plagues many other technically-deep PS in this batch.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: True robustness across genuinely diverse unstructured scenarios (the actual research challenge) is hard to fully demonstrate in 36 hours, scope to a focused set of representative scenarios rather than claiming general robustness.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm your team has genuine simulation/robotics experience (ideally with MATLAB/Simulink or a comparable framework) before committing, this PS rewards real technical depth, not surface-level implementation.

idea_0_4: Choose 3-4 representative unstructured-road scenarios to simulate (e.g. mixed vehicle types at an unmarked intersection, a pedestrian crossing unpredictably, a pothole/obstacle avoidance case).
Set up your simulation environment (MATLAB/Simulink or comparable) and basic sensor model.
Split: one person on perception/sensor simulation, one on the planning/collision-avoidance algorithm.
prototype_4_22: Build the multi-sensor perception simulation for your chosen scenarios.
Build the core adaptive path-planning algorithm.
Start the collision-avoidance logic layered on top of planning.
integration_22_30: Connect perception -> planning -> collision avoidance in your simulation environment.
Test against all your chosen representative scenarios, not just the easiest one.
Compare against a standard (non-adaptive) planning approach to quantify the improvement in unstructured conditions.
polish_30_36: Build clear visualizations of your simulation results, this is a technically dense topic, visual clarity matters for the demo.
Rehearse walking through each representative scenario and why your adaptive approach handles it better than standard planning.
Prepare to discuss the gap between your simulated scenarios and full real-world robustness honestly.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Run a side-by-side simulation comparison live, standard planning failing or struggling on an unstructured scenario versus your adaptive system handling it, that visual contrast makes the technical achievement concrete for judges.

strengths: Explicitly simulation-based, removing hardware/physical-build risk entirely.
Addresses a genuine, actively-researched gap specific to Indian road conditions.
weaknesses: Requires real robotics/simulation expertise on the team, not broadly accessible to a general software team.
Full generalizable robustness across all unstructured scenarios isn't demonstrable in 36 hours, must be scoped to representative cases.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Robotics-skill-heavy, this PS is not accessible to a general web/app development team.
team_fit.approach: Confirm real simulation/robotics experience on the team before committing, this is one of the more technically specialized PS in the batch.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Basic simulation environment scaffolding and standard sensor-model boilerplate.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: The actual adaptive planning algorithm design for genuinely unpredictable, mixed-traffic scenarios, this requires real robotics domain expertise, not a default planning algorithm.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded planning algorithm that works on the easy scenarios but fails on the genuinely unstructured ones would miss the entire point of the PS, which is specifically about handling that unpredictability.

data_resource_availability.status: No real Indian-road sensor dataset is required for a simulation-based approach, this is inherently a simulated-environment task.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Not applicable, the simulation itself is the deliverable, not real-world data collection.

judge_qna.question: How does your adaptive system actually differ from standard autonomous path planning, beyond just working on different scenarios?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Point to the specific adaptive mechanism, how your system updates its planning in real time based on the perceived uncertainty level, versus a standard system's fixed assumptions about structured traffic.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the computational cost of that adaptiveness, is it fast enough for real-time use?

judge_qna.question: How confident are you this would generalize beyond your chosen test scenarios?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be honest about the scope, you tested against representative unstructured scenarios, true generalization would need extensive real-world validation beyond hackathon scope, but your approach's underlying adaptiveness principle would extend.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the failure mode when your system encounters a scenario type it wasn't tested against?
